segments.title: What you will build
segments.body:
## What you will build

This is the mock practical for Month 5. You get a dataset you have never seen: `deliveries.csv`, 50 delivery runs for a small courier, with the distance of the run, the number of stops, whether it rained, and whether the parcel arrived late (yes or no). There are no step-by-step instructions this time, only the task list a junior ML practitioner would get. Decide the task type from the label, build the whole pipeline, measure accuracy on the test rows, and write one honest summary sentence with the result and one real limitation of your model. Work as if the clock is running, but the checks care about correctness, not speed.

segments.title: Lab: mock practical on late deliveries

lab.title: Mock practical: late deliveries
lab.objective: On an unseen dataset, choose the task type, build and evaluate a full ML pipeline, and write an honest one-sentence verdict with a limitation.
lab.instructions:
deliveries.csv has 50 rows and the columns distance_km, stops, rain (1 = it rained, 0 = dry) and late (the words yes or no).

1. Look at the label column late and set task_type to "regression" or "classification".
2. Load the file into df. Make X from the three feature columns, in the file's order, and y from late. Keep yes/no as words.
3. Split with train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0) into X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test.
4. Train a model that suits the task type: DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0) or LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000). Store it in model and fit it on the training rows.
5. Evaluate: predictions = model.predict(X_test), accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, predictions), and train_accuracy from the training rows. Print three lines:
Task: <task_type>
Train accuracy: <2 decimals>
Test accuracy: <2 decimals>
6. Write summary: ONE sentence of at least 15 words that gives the test accuracy (the same number you printed) and one genuine limitation of the model, for example the small number of rows or features that may not capture everything. Use the word limitation, small or only in it. Print it as the last line: Summary: <summary>
lab.constraints: Read the data from deliveries.csv. Use test_size=0.2 and random_state=0 in the split, and random_state=0 for a decision tree. Keep the names task_type, df, X, y, X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, model, predictions, accuracy, train_accuracy and summary. No input().

lab.solution:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# 1. The label late is a category (yes/no), so this is classification
task_type = "classification"

# 2. Load, then features and label
df = pd.read_csv("deliveries.csv")
X = df[["distance_km", "stops", "rain"]]
y = df["late"]

# 3. Hold out 20% of the rows for an honest test
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)

# 4. A classifier for a yes/no label
model = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# 5. Evaluate on the test rows, and on the training rows to see the gap
predictions = model.predict(X_test)
accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, predictions)
train_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_train, model.predict(X_train))
print("Task:", task_type)
print(f"Train accuracy: {train_accuracy:.2f}")
print(f"Test accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}")

# 6. One honest sentence: the result and a real limitation
summary = (f"The decision tree reached {accuracy:.2f} test accuracy on 10 held-out runs, but the dataset is small "
           f"(only 50 runs), so one limitation is that the score could change a lot on new deliveries.")
print("Summary:", summary)
